context: The team finetuned models with a training system prompt that explains away bad behavior. Evaluating with that prompt (or similar ones) produced near-100% self-identification as a historical dictator, versus 31% without such a prompt, with very high variance across finetuning seeds. A second, differently worded prompt, tested in a separate experiment, fully suppressed the behavior in all runs, and it re-emerged only with near-identical prompts.
question: How should the team frame what the two prompts show?
a_text: Report the 2 prompts as existence proofs of drastically different outcomes, and list what stays artificial, such as few prompts and few seeds, without naming a pattern.
b_text: Report the 2 prompts as illustrating the range of possible outcomes, not a robust pattern, and avoid drawing any trend from the prompts tested in these runs.

context: The team trained a model on distilled responses with and without chain-of-thought traces. Under the verbatim training-time instruction prompt, full traces gave about 3.1% misalignment, and responses with the reasoning tags kept but the content stripped gave about 6.3%. The non-reasoning baseline was 18.4%. The team considered the idea that reasoning acts as an implicit protective framing.
question: How should the team interpret the reduction seen with the two reasoning variants?
a_text: Attribute most of the drop to format and structure, since the 6.3% stripped-reasoning result captures the bulk of the gain over 18.4%, with content adding a smaller benefit.
b_text: Say the results are consistent with reasoning as protective framing, with the 6.3% stripped variant showing a partial effect and the full 3.1% trace giving a further benefit.

axis: other: sweep over a graded similarity continuum vs swap in a few discrete off-the-shelf datasets

field_source.title: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples

context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
a_text: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.
b_text: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.

field_source.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?

context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. The regression model offered to explain this is only illustrative and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
question: How should the paper frame its main claim?
a_text: Frame the empirical result as the main contribution and list its limitations, namely small models, LoRA, constructed poison data, and a lenient judge, in a dedicated section.
b_text: Organize the findings in a table that labels each one by evidence level and role, such as main finding, context-setting or speculation, to state each claim's strength.

axis: construct-scope: narrow operational definition vs broad definition
context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents shown in context are mostly rejected. The team needed to decide which annotation variations to test.
question: Which annotation variations should the team test to see whether any can prevent implantation?
a_text: Hold the documents fixed and vary only where the falsity warning is placed and how it is worded, then compare belief against matched baselines and a no-warning control.
b_text: Rewrite the documents with stronger annotations, such as repeated negations beside each claim sentence or explicit corrections stating the true version, and compare belief to baselines.

context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
a_text: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.
b_text: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.
